newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian socialist nominee suggests coalition.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian socialist nominee suggests coalition.

text.p: Bulgarian Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the ruling Socialists' nominee for premier, proposed on Friday that President Petar Stoyanov appoint a coalition government to bring the country out of crisis.

After nearly four weeks of daily mass protests against the Socialists' plans to form a new cabinet, Dobrev told Reuters the crisis had now got beyond party politics and he would be willing to give up his mandate for the sake of consensus.
"I think the country now needs a constitutional government on a very wide political base," he said in an interview.

"I don't mind if it is formed under the leadership of the president as I highly respect the president's efforts to find a way out of the crisis," he said. "I am ready to return my mandate if such a government is formed."
The Socialists' opponents have held 26 consecutive days of street protests fuelled by an economic crisis that has sent the national currency into freefall.
Stoyanov, a pro-market liberal, was obliged to give the Socialists, as the largest party in parliament, a mandate to form a new government after his efforts to mediate a compromise failed.
Returning from a visit to Brussels on Friday, the president renewed his call for immediate elections and said Dobrev should give up the mandate.
Dobrev and Stoyanov were expected to meet later on Friday.
"Neither of the two political forces can solve the problems of the country by itself," Dobrev said. "We need a national political effort to lead the country out of crisis."

The opposition held one session of talks with the Socialists under Stoyanov's mediation last week and refused to meet them again, saying dialogue was impossible. They have ruled out joining any coalition cabinet led by Dobrev.
"They want to keep up their hard line," Dobrev said. "They are debating their position only in the media and in the streets."
The opposition has proposed a caretaker cabinet and immediate elections, but Dobrev said such a cabinet could not negotiate with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
He said he agreed with the position of the European Union that the priorities were to agree on the timing of elections, set up a broad-based government and renew talks with the IMF.

Dobrev said the new cabinet should prepare the laws needed for introduction of a strict fixed exchange rate regime to halt the collapse of the national currency, draw up a state budget for 1997 and adopt anti-crisis measures that had the support of all parties.
"I see elections at the end of the summer or the beginning of the autumn, not for political reasons but for social and economic reasons," Dobrev said.

The Socialists were elected in December 1994 and formally have nearly two years of their term left, but protesters have taken to the streets nationwide for 26 consecutive days to demand immediate elections.
Dobrev said Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov also supported any effort to find a consensus, but there were factions in the party who opposed him.
"There are elements who are resisting but I don't think it's an important issue," he said. "I think the most important is that my position is good for Bulgaria, not for politics."
